medical.title: How psychedelics could deliver antidepressant benefits without hallucinogenic effects
medical.summary: Could psychedelics become a new generation of treatments for depression and other psychiatric disorders? This question is no longer confined to basic research. Several therapies based on classical psychedelics have advanced into late-stage clinical development and have reported encouraging results. DT120, an LSD-based candidate, and COMP360, a synthetic psilocybin formulation, have both received breakthrough therapy designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

medical.title: How insurance coverage shapes access to kidney transplantation
medical.summary: For people with kidney failure, access to transplantation can mean better survival and quality of life.

medical.title: Xenon-based method measures key MRI contrast metal more sensitively than earlier techniques
medical.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, provides detailed images of the inside of the body. It is an indispensable procedure for the diagnosis and treatment planning of many types of cancer, and it does not expose the body to radiation because it uses magnetic fields and low-energy radio waves. Pathological changes, such as tumors, can be clearly distinguished from healthy tissue in MRI images.

medical.title: Spinal cord injury can reshape gut microbes that influence whole-body health
medical.summary: Scientists exploring the links between a spinal cord injury, inflammation and immune function have turned their attention to a genome-level analysis of the gut microbial community, with early study results offering hints at potential new approaches to aid healing.

medical.title: Tumor mutations and immune activity may reveal who benefits from investigational lymphoma drug
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba conducted a physician-initiated phase 2 clinical trial of dasatinib in patients with relapsed or refractory T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (TFHL), an aggressive and difficult-to-treat blood cancer. The study identified genetic alterations and features of the immune microenvironment associated with treatment response. These findings may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit from dasatinib and inform the development of personalized treatment strategies and novel immunotherapeutic approaches. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

medical.title: Common gut virus infects bacteria—not human cells
medical.summary: Thriving alongside trillions of bacteria in the human digestive tract is a vast population of viruses. Ever since one such denizen of the gut microbiome, known as picobirnavirus, was first spotted decades ago, researchers thought it directly infected human tissue and played a role in gastrointestinal illness. But researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and collaborators have just rewritten that story: This widespread virus infects gut bacteria, not human cells.

medical.title: Ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime help resistant bacteria thrive in hospital sewage
medical.summary: Antibiotics excreted by patients promote antibiotic-resistant bacteria in hospital sewers, according to a new study by researchers at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden. Ultimately, this may contribute to the development and spread of hard-to-treat infections. Pinpointing the responsible antibiotics paves the way for targeted measures.

medical.title: Heat waves and pollution increase stroke risk in older adults, study finds
medical.summary: A study conducted in Brazil by researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) found that each additional day spent under a heat wave in São Paulo is associated with an increased risk of acute stroke in people ages 65 and older. For the research, a heat wave was defined as at least two consecutive days with maximum temperatures of 33.1 °C (92 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher.

medical.title: COMPASS pathway enables regulatory T cells to prevent devastating autoimmune responses to gut bacteria
medical.summary: Trillions of bacteria live in the human gut without triggering an immune response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have now discovered a gene-regulatory pathway that helps maintain this delicate balance. In a study published in Science Advances, they show that regulatory T cells, a type of immune cell, co-opt a well-known general gene expression pathway called COMPASS to suppress inappropriate immune responses and prevent lethal inflammation and autoimmunity.

medical.title: Blood test offers new way to track lung cancer
medical.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists and collaborators have demonstrated a novel liquid biopsy technique that can measure cancer burden and reveal molecular characteristics of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), according to a new study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

medical.title: Healthy diet may lower heart disease risk after cancer
medical.summary: Eating a healthy diet is associated with a reduced risk of heart disease and death among cancer survivors, according to a study published today in JACC: Advances.

medical.title: Specialized immune cells may help skin nimbly respond to changing environmental conditions
medical.summary: As the steadfast protector of the body's interior, the skin must be able to swiftly respond to stressors from the outside world and then return to a steady state to maintain everyday operations. Coordinating that agile response are epidermal stem cells (EpSCs), which initiate development of specialized skin cells sent to the surface while also maintaining a ready pool of new stem cells to draw from.

medical.title: Premature birth alters the brain's developmental clock
medical.summary: A new study reveals that when a baby is born prematurely, their cerebellum, the part of the brain with a critical role in motor function, language and cognition, grows and develops in a different way than it would if the baby remained in utero to full term.

medical.title: Antibody candidate could help preserve appetite and muscle strength in patients with cancer
medical.summary: In cancer cachexia, patients continue to lose weight, muscle and fat even when they eat. A KAIST research team has developed a therapeutic candidate that blocks a signal responsible for appetite suppression, weight loss and excessive energy expenditure.

medical.title: Lower serum total calcium linked to postdischarge outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
medical.summary: For hospitalized patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), low serum total calcium is associated with a reduced risk for heart failure readmission, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular events after discharge, according to a study published online Sept. 28 in Biomedicines.

medical.title: 5 calisthenics moves for a full-body workout you can do anywhere
medical.summary: Whether you realize it or not, you're probably already familiar with calisthenics. Put simply, calisthenics is just bodyweight exercises. Calisthenics is great for beginners because it builds full-body strength and requires no equipment. You can also easily modify exercises for different levels of difficulty.

medical.title: STI screening linked to fewer preterm births
medical.summary: Screening and treating pregnant patients for three common sexually transmitted infections (STIs) twice during pregnancy was associated with a 23% lower risk of preterm birth compared with standard care, according to a randomized clinical trial published in Clinical Infectious Diseases from researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Southern California.

medical.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

medical.title: Scientists discover why some people still can’t taste food after COVID-19
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for why some people struggle to taste food more than a year after recovering from COVID-19. By examining taste buds from patients with lingering symptoms, researchers discovered molecular abnormalities that weaken the signals responsible for detecting sweet, bitter, and savory flavors.

medical.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
medical.summary: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

medical.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
medical.summary: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

medical.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

medical.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
medical.summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.

science.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
science.summary: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

science.title: Qinghai–Tibet Plateau study traces evolution of terrestrial animals across three distinct regions
science.summary: A new study has pieced together the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), offering a comprehensive picture of how the distinctive fauna of the "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.

science.title: The human surfaceome: AI flags potential cell surface drug targets overlooked by major databases
science.summary: More than 65% of approved medicines work by binding to proteins on the surface of human cells. Yet scientists developing new treatments face a fundamental problem: Major biological databases disagree about which proteins are actually found on cell surfaces.

science.title: Halloween Aboard the International Space Station
science.summary: Although no ghouls, goblins, or trick-or-treaters come knocking at the International Space Station’s front hatch, crew members aboard the orbiting laboratory still like to get in the Halloween spirit. Whether individually or as an entire crew, they dress up in sometimes spooky, sometimes scary, but always creative costumes, often designed from materials available aboard the […]

science.title: Nature finance needs a fundamental rethink, researchers argue
science.summary: The authors call on governments, investors and conservation organizers to reimagine nature finance based on a central tenet: raising funds should be a means to an end, not an end in itself.

science.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
science.summary: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

science.title: Detailed images reveal ribosome assembly inside human cells for the first time
science.summary: For decades, ribosomes have been under the lens of many scientists. Ribosomes are highly sophisticated and complex molecular machines that allow cells to synthesize proteins. However, putting ribosomes together requires intricate assembly processes. While many underlying mechanisms for building ribosomes have been discovered ex situ (outside their native cellular context), our understanding of how ribosomes are assembled in situ has so far remained limited.

science.title: Eyewitnesses remember feedback better after making an identification, study finds
science.summary: An eyewitness can tell the truth, believe every word they say and still send an innocent person to prison. A new study by Stephen Charman from FIU's Department of Psychology takes on a question that has challenged the justice system for decades: Can we rely on eyewitnesses to help identify the person responsible for a crime?

science.title: Terahertz light distinguishes two groups of particles trapped inside superconducting vortices
science.summary: Scientists at Rutgers and in Estonia have used invisible light to look into tiny magnetic whirlpools, called vortices, inside a superconductor, revealing details that could help researchers develop better materials for carrying electricity.

science.title: What animal bones in Malawi teach us about the social lives of people long ago
science.summary: In the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next?

science.title: European rivers retain far more plastic than they carry to the sea, study finds
science.summary: Plastic that enters the environment does not necessarily make its way to the sea via rivers. In fact, only a tiny fraction eventually reaches river mouths. Most plastic remains on land or within river systems.

science.title: Wild orchids face growing challenges as conservation falls short
science.summary: At first glance, it is easy to see why Corybas puniceus has captured the attention of collectors around the world. Small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, its unusual shape and bursts of color make it unlike almost anything else in the orchid world. The species, found only in Southeast Asia, is classified as critically endangered.

science.title: How eggs protect chromosome connections during prolonged dormancy
science.summary: Eggs follow a very different developmental path from sperm. Once a male hits puberty, sperm cells are produced continuously throughout his life. Eggs, however, are all produced during the fetal stage. Once formed, eggs enter a long dormant state called the dictyate stage, in which the process of cell division (meiosis) is paused partway through. This dormant period ends only when the egg is ovulated.

science.title: Machine learning helps track semiconductor defects under more realistic temperature conditions
science.summary: All materials contain inherent defects. These are not always harmful, since they can be used to engineer and introduce certain properties into a material. However, it is crucial to understand how they function and how they affect the material's properties.

science.title: Machine-learning models predict human health from microbiome data
science.summary: Inside the gut, on the surface of the skin and lining your ears, mouth and nose are colonies of millions of microbes. For every human cell you have, there are at least as many microbial cells associated with your body.

science.title: Nanoparticle properties shape protein coats that guide cell entry and immune evasion
science.summary: A new study has revealed molecular rules governing how nanoparticles interact with biological systems, showing how their physicochemical properties shape protein corona (PC) formation and influence biological outcomes. The findings provide a framework for designing nanomedicines with more predictable biological identities.

science.title: Fingerprints of the sea: Identifying sharks by their fins alone
science.summary: Every oceanic whitetip shark has a fin pattern as unique as a human fingerprint. In a new study published in Marine Biology, FIU researchers identified more than 50 oceanic whitetip sharks by their fins alone using pelagic baited remote underwater video stations, pBRUVS, off the coast of Cat Island, the Bahamas.

science.title: Snøfrid the Sámi: Matriarch of Norway's royal bloodline?
science.summary: For a long time, some researchers believed that the South Sámi population arrived in Central Norway in the 18th century at the earliest, and that Norwegian farmers were present long before the Sámi. This is known as the "hypothesis of late immigration."

science.title: Light-emitting nanoparticles help ultrasound direct gene editing to selected mouse brain regions
science.summary: Scientists can now edit genes in precise locations deep in the brain and body without the use of invasive surgery or implants, thanks to new work from researchers at the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute. The team demonstrated its technique, which uses a combination of ultrasound, light-emitting nanoparticles and photo-controllable gene-editing proteins, by successfully altering genes in mouse brains at selected locations.

science.title: Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent
science.summary: After the United Nations adopted a resolution in September 2026 endorsing a map that more fairly represents the size of Earth's landmasses, author and journalist Moky Makura of Africa No Filter—a main sponsor of the Correct the Map initiative—asked: "What else about Africa is the world underestimating that's also hidden in plain sight?"

science.title: Zombie bacteria keep building DNA after death
science.summary: Researchers at Aarhus University have discovered that bacteria can continue producing DNA after they die. And they have found a way to control what gets produced. The discovery could eventually contribute to the development of new biological materials.

science.title: Electrical signals reveal hidden magnetic information in altermagnets for first time
science.summary: Researchers have experimentally demonstrated, for the first time, that it is possible to obtain from an altermagnet a spin current that can transport magnetic information. This result is supported by the theoretical model of electron transport developed by the CFM group. Altermagnets are a new class of materials that, despite not exhibiting the net magnetization characteristic of conventional magnets, can generate this type of current.

science.title: Newly discovered amoeba reproduces at 145 F, breaking heat record for eukaryotic life
science.summary: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.

science.title: Planetary collisions may help young worlds hold on to their atmospheres
science.summary: A new study lets some of the air out of a long-held theory that growing, rocky planets will lose their atmosphere if they smash into a large object in space.

science.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
science.summary: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […]

environment.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
environment.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

environment.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
environment.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

environment.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
environment.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

environment.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
environment.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

environment.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
environment.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

environment.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
environment.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
environment.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

environment.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
environment.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

environment.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
environment.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

environment.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

environment.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
environment.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

mix_items.title: Elveţia ia în calcul reducerea vitezei maxime pe autostrăzile sale la 80 km/h. Motivul pentru care s-ar putea lua această decizie
mix_items.summary: Elveţia ia în calcul o reducere temporară a vitezei pe autostrăzi, o măsură care ar veni să „completeze măsurile luate deja pentru economisirea de combustibil, potrivit Oficiului Federal pentru Aprovizionarea Economică a Ţării, relatează Le Figaro.

mix_items.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
mix_items.summary: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea Alinei și cum sprijinul oferit de Fundația Inocenți a ajutat-o să își dezvolte încrederea în sine, abilitățile școlare și curajul de a reuși. mix_items.title: How psychedelics could deliver antidepressant benefits without hallucinogenic effects
mix_items.summary: Could psychedelics become a new generation of treatments for depression and other psychiatric disorders? This question is no longer confined to basic research. Several therapies based on classical psychedelics have advanced into late-stage clinical development and have reported encouraging results. DT120, an LSD-based candidate, and COMP360, a synthetic psilocybin formulation, have both received breakthrough therapy designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

mix_items.title: Qinghai–Tibet Plateau study traces evolution of terrestrial animals across three distinct regions
mix_items.summary: A new study has pieced together the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), offering a comprehensive picture of how the distinctive fauna of the "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.

mix_items.title: The human surfaceome: AI flags potential cell surface drug targets overlooked by major databases
mix_items.summary: More than 65% of approved medicines work by binding to proteins on the surface of human cells. Yet scientists developing new treatments face a fundamental problem: Major biological databases disagree about which proteins are actually found on cell surfaces.

mix_items.title: Halloween Aboard the International Space Station
mix_items.summary: Although no ghouls, goblins, or trick-or-treaters come knocking at the International Space Station’s front hatch, crew members aboard the orbiting laboratory still like to get in the Halloween spirit. Whether individually or as an entire crew, they dress up in sometimes spooky, sometimes scary, but always creative costumes, often designed from materials available aboard the […]

mix_items.title: How insurance coverage shapes access to kidney transplantation
mix_items.summary: For people with kidney failure, access to transplantation can mean better survival and quality of life.

mix_items.title: Nature finance needs a fundamental rethink, researchers argue
mix_items.summary: The authors call on governments, investors and conservation organizers to reimagine nature finance based on a central tenet: raising funds should be a means to an end, not an end in itself.

mix_items.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
mix_items.summary: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

mix_items.title: Detailed images reveal ribosome assembly inside human cells for the first time
mix_items.summary: For decades, ribosomes have been under the lens of many scientists. Ribosomes are highly sophisticated and complex molecular machines that allow cells to synthesize proteins. However, putting ribosomes together requires intricate assembly processes. While many underlying mechanisms for building ribosomes have been discovered ex situ (outside their native cellular context), our understanding of how ribosomes are assembled in situ has so far remained limited.

mix_items.title: Eyewitnesses remember feedback better after making an identification, study finds
mix_items.summary: An eyewitness can tell the truth, believe every word they say and still send an innocent person to prison. A new study by Stephen Charman from FIU's Department of Psychology takes on a question that has challenged the justice system for decades: Can we rely on eyewitnesses to help identify the person responsible for a crime?

mix_items.title: Xenon-based method measures key MRI contrast metal more sensitively than earlier techniques
mix_items.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, provides detailed images of the inside of the body. It is an indispensable procedure for the diagnosis and treatment planning of many types of cancer, and it does not expose the body to radiation because it uses magnetic fields and low-energy radio waves. Pathological changes, such as tumors, can be clearly distinguished from healthy tissue in MRI images.

mix_items.title: Terahertz light distinguishes two groups of particles trapped inside superconducting vortices
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Rutgers and in Estonia have used invisible light to look into tiny magnetic whirlpools, called vortices, inside a superconductor, revealing details that could help researchers develop better materials for carrying electricity.

mix_items.title: What animal bones in Malawi teach us about the social lives of people long ago
mix_items.summary: In the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next?

mix_items.title: European rivers retain far more plastic than they carry to the sea, study finds
mix_items.summary: Plastic that enters the environment does not necessarily make its way to the sea via rivers. In fact, only a tiny fraction eventually reaches river mouths. Most plastic remains on land or within river systems.

mix_items.title: Spinal cord injury can reshape gut microbes that influence whole-body health
mix_items.summary: Scientists exploring the links between a spinal cord injury, inflammation and immune function have turned their attention to a genome-level analysis of the gut microbial community, with early study results offering hints at potential new approaches to aid healing.

mix_items.title: Wild orchids face growing challenges as conservation falls short
mix_items.summary: At first glance, it is easy to see why Corybas puniceus has captured the attention of collectors around the world. Small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, its unusual shape and bursts of color make it unlike almost anything else in the orchid world. The species, found only in Southeast Asia, is classified as critically endangered.

mix_items.title: How eggs protect chromosome connections during prolonged dormancy
mix_items.summary: Eggs follow a very different developmental path from sperm. Once a male hits puberty, sperm cells are produced continuously throughout his life. Eggs, however, are all produced during the fetal stage. Once formed, eggs enter a long dormant state called the dictyate stage, in which the process of cell division (meiosis) is paused partway through. This dormant period ends only when the egg is ovulated.

mix_items.title: Machine learning helps track semiconductor defects under more realistic temperature conditions
mix_items.summary: All materials contain inherent defects. These are not always harmful, since they can be used to engineer and introduce certain properties into a material. However, it is crucial to understand how they function and how they affect the material's properties.

mix_items.title: Machine-learning models predict human health from microbiome data
mix_items.summary: Inside the gut, on the surface of the skin and lining your ears, mouth and nose are colonies of millions of microbes. For every human cell you have, there are at least as many microbial cells associated with your body.

mix_items.title: Tumor mutations and immune activity may reveal who benefits from investigational lymphoma drug
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Tsukuba conducted a physician-initiated phase 2 clinical trial of dasatinib in patients with relapsed or refractory T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (TFHL), an aggressive and difficult-to-treat blood cancer. The study identified genetic alterations and features of the immune microenvironment associated with treatment response. These findings may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit from dasatinib and inform the development of personalized treatment strategies and novel immunotherapeutic approaches. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Nanoparticle properties shape protein coats that guide cell entry and immune evasion
mix_items.summary: A new study has revealed molecular rules governing how nanoparticles interact with biological systems, showing how their physicochemical properties shape protein corona (PC) formation and influence biological outcomes. The findings provide a framework for designing nanomedicines with more predictable biological identities.

mix_items.title: Fingerprints of the sea: Identifying sharks by their fins alone
mix_items.summary: Every oceanic whitetip shark has a fin pattern as unique as a human fingerprint. In a new study published in Marine Biology, FIU researchers identified more than 50 oceanic whitetip sharks by their fins alone using pelagic baited remote underwater video stations, pBRUVS, off the coast of Cat Island, the Bahamas.

mix_items.title: Snøfrid the Sámi: Matriarch of Norway's royal bloodline?
mix_items.summary: For a long time, some researchers believed that the South Sámi population arrived in Central Norway in the 18th century at the earliest, and that Norwegian farmers were present long before the Sámi. This is known as the "hypothesis of late immigration."

mix_items.title: Common gut virus infects bacteria—not human cells
mix_items.summary: Thriving alongside trillions of bacteria in the human digestive tract is a vast population of viruses. Ever since one such denizen of the gut microbiome, known as picobirnavirus, was first spotted decades ago, researchers thought it directly infected human tissue and played a role in gastrointestinal illness. But researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and collaborators have just rewritten that story: This widespread virus infects gut bacteria, not human cells.

mix_items.title: Light-emitting nanoparticles help ultrasound direct gene editing to selected mouse brain regions
mix_items.summary: Scientists can now edit genes in precise locations deep in the brain and body without the use of invasive surgery or implants, thanks to new work from researchers at the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute. The team demonstrated its technique, which uses a combination of ultrasound, light-emitting nanoparticles and photo-controllable gene-editing proteins, by successfully altering genes in mouse brains at selected locations.

mix_items.title: Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent
mix_items.summary: After the United Nations adopted a resolution in September 2026 endorsing a map that more fairly represents the size of Earth's landmasses, author and journalist Moky Makura of Africa No Filter—a main sponsor of the Correct the Map initiative—asked: "What else about Africa is the world underestimating that's also hidden in plain sight?"

mix_items.title: Zombie bacteria keep building DNA after death
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Aarhus University have discovered that bacteria can continue producing DNA after they die. And they have found a way to control what gets produced. The discovery could eventually contribute to the development of new biological materials.

mix_items.title: Ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime help resistant bacteria thrive in hospital sewage
mix_items.summary: Antibiotics excreted by patients promote antibiotic-resistant bacteria in hospital sewers, according to a new study by researchers at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden. Ultimately, this may contribute to the development and spread of hard-to-treat infections. Pinpointing the responsible antibiotics paves the way for targeted measures.

mix_items.title: Heat waves and pollution increase stroke risk in older adults, study finds
mix_items.summary: A study conducted in Brazil by researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) found that each additional day spent under a heat wave in São Paulo is associated with an increased risk of acute stroke in people ages 65 and older. For the research, a heat wave was defined as at least two consecutive days with maximum temperatures of 33.1 °C (92 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher.

mix_items.title: Electrical signals reveal hidden magnetic information in altermagnets for first time
mix_items.summary: Researchers have experimentally demonstrated, for the first time, that it is possible to obtain from an altermagnet a spin current that can transport magnetic information. This result is supported by the theoretical model of electron transport developed by the CFM group. Altermagnets are a new class of materials that, despite not exhibiting the net magnetization characteristic of conventional magnets, can generate this type of current.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered amoeba reproduces at 145 F, breaking heat record for eukaryotic life
mix_items.summary: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.

mix_items.title: Planetary collisions may help young worlds hold on to their atmospheres
mix_items.summary: A new study lets some of the air out of a long-held theory that growing, rocky planets will lose their atmosphere if they smash into a large object in space.

mix_items.title: COMPASS pathway enables regulatory T cells to prevent devastating autoimmune responses to gut bacteria
mix_items.summary: Trillions of bacteria live in the human gut without triggering an immune response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have now discovered a gene-regulatory pathway that helps maintain this delicate balance. In a study published in Science Advances, they show that regulatory T cells, a type of immune cell, co-opt a well-known general gene expression pathway called COMPASS to suppress inappropriate immune responses and prevent lethal inflammation and autoimmunity.

mix_items.title: Blood test offers new way to track lung cancer
mix_items.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists and collaborators have demonstrated a novel liquid biopsy technique that can measure cancer burden and reveal molecular characteristics of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), according to a new study published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

mix_items.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
mix_items.summary: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one […]

mix_items.title: Healthy diet may lower heart disease risk after cancer
mix_items.summary: Eating a healthy diet is associated with a reduced risk of heart disease and death among cancer survivors, according to a study published today in JACC: Advances.

mix_items.title: Specialized immune cells may help skin nimbly respond to changing environmental conditions
mix_items.summary: As the steadfast protector of the body's interior, the skin must be able to swiftly respond to stressors from the outside world and then return to a steady state to maintain everyday operations. Coordinating that agile response are epidermal stem cells (EpSCs), which initiate development of specialized skin cells sent to the surface while also maintaining a ready pool of new stem cells to draw from.

mix_items.title: Premature birth alters the brain's developmental clock
mix_items.summary: A new study reveals that when a baby is born prematurely, their cerebellum, the part of the brain with a critical role in motor function, language and cognition, grows and develops in a different way than it would if the baby remained in utero to full term.

mix_items.title: Antibody candidate could help preserve appetite and muscle strength in patients with cancer
mix_items.summary: In cancer cachexia, patients continue to lose weight, muscle and fat even when they eat. A KAIST research team has developed a therapeutic candidate that blocks a signal responsible for appetite suppression, weight loss and excessive energy expenditure.

mix_items.title: Lower serum total calcium linked to postdischarge outcomes in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
mix_items.summary: For hospitalized patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), low serum total calcium is associated with a reduced risk for heart failure readmission, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular events after discharge, according to a study published online Sept. 28 in Biomedicines.

mix_items.title: 5 calisthenics moves for a full-body workout you can do anywhere
mix_items.summary: Whether you realize it or not, you're probably already familiar with calisthenics. Put simply, calisthenics is just bodyweight exercises. Calisthenics is great for beginners because it builds full-body strength and requires no equipment. You can also easily modify exercises for different levels of difficulty.

mix_items.title: STI screening linked to fewer preterm births
mix_items.summary: Screening and treating pregnant patients for three common sexually transmitted infections (STIs) twice during pregnancy was associated with a 23% lower risk of preterm birth compared with standard care, according to a randomized clinical trial published in Clinical Infectious Diseases from researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and University of Southern California.

mix_items.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
mix_items.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

mix_items.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
mix_items.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

mix_items.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
mix_items.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

mix_items.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
mix_items.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

mix_items.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
mix_items.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

mix_items.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
mix_items.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

mix_items.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover why some people still can’t taste food after COVID-19
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for why some people struggle to taste food more than a year after recovering from COVID-19. By examining taste buds from patients with lingering symptoms, researchers discovered molecular abnormalities that weaken the signals responsible for detecting sweet, bitter, and savory flavors.

mix_items.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
mix_items.summary: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

mix_items.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
mix_items.summary: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

mix_items.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

mix_items.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
mix_items.summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
mix_items.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

mix_items.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
mix_items.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

mix_items.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
mix_items.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
mix_items.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
